name: Cryptography Toolkit & Cryptoanalysis
tagline: Decode/encode data, identify encodings, and break weak ciphers and RSA on materials you own: CTF crypto, historical ciphers, and flawed implementations. Password recovery lives in 'passwords'.

tools.name: CyberChef
tools.desc: GCHQ's browser 'Cyber Swiss Army Knife': 480+ chainable operations for decoding/encoding (Base64, hex, URL, Rot13), hashing, XOR and compression, plus the Magic operation that auto-detects and unwraps multi-layer encodings. Entirely client-side, zero install.
tools.when: First stop for any blob, hex dump or encoded string: click the Magic icon to auto-decode, then drag operations to peel off the layers you identify.

tools.name: CyberChef (self-hosted)
tools.desc: The same GCHQ app run from the official pre-built Docker image (or a downloadable static build) so every operation executes inside your own network with no outbound traffic.
tools.when: Offline, air-gapped or VM work where the input must never leave your machine - identical recipes and Magic, no internet dependency after the image pull.

tools.name: hashID
tools.desc: Python 3 tool identifying 220+ hash types by regex and reporting the matching hashcat mode (-m) and John format (-j) for each candidate, replacing the outdated hash-identifier.
tools.when: Any recovered hash before cracking: feed it the value, note the top algorithm plus its hashcat/John mode, then jump to the passwords domain.

tools.name: file (libmagic)
tools.desc: The standard `file` command built on libmagic: identifies thousands of file types from magic bytes, from PEM/DER keys and PKCS#12 bundles to plaintext/uncompressed containers.
tools.when: Determine what a raw blob actually is before decoding — distinguish a DER key, a zlib stream, a base64 text, or a random-looking ciphertext file.
tools.install: sudo apt install file && file suspect.bin

tools.name: dCode
tools.desc: Web reference hosting hundreds of small solvers for classical schemes (Caesar, Vigenère, Enigma, ADFGVX, Playfair...) plus a Cipher Identifier that scores which of 300+ ciphers a message fits via n-gram and index-of-coincidence analysis.
tools.when: CTF or challenge text in a historical cipher: paste it into the Cipher Identifier for a ranked guess, then open the matching solver for the plaintext.

tools.name: CrypTool
tools.desc: Legacy university/open-source cryptology suite (CrypTool 2.1 + JCrypTool) for experimenting with classical ciphers (Caesar, Vigenère, Enigma, ADFGVX) and their built-in automated cryptanalysis on paste-in text.
tools.when: Interactive analysis of historical substitution/transposition ciphers or learning the attack against a classical scheme on your own text, where a GUI beats hand-rolled scripts.

tools.name: xortool
tools.desc: Python tool for multi-byte XOR cipher analysis: guesses key length via equality-based scoring, recovers key bytes from the most frequent plaintext character, with charset filtering and known-plaintext (-p) options to confirm candidates.
tools.when: Ciphertext is XOR-encoded with an unknown repeating key - feed the raw bytes, let it rank key lengths, then solve for the right length and character.

tools.name: cribdrag
tools.desc: Interactive crib-dragging script for stream-cipher keystream reuse: XOR two ciphertexts (or against a guessed crib) and step through candidate plaintext substrings interactively.
tools.when: Two ciphertexts share a one-time pad key, or a stream cipher reuses its keystream — drag a known plaintext word to recover the keystream and decrypt the rest by hand.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/SpiderLabs/cribdrag && python2 cribdrag.py encrypted.hex

tools.name: PadBuster
tools.desc: Perl script automating padding-oracle attacks: decrypts arbitrary CBC ciphertext, encrypts arbitrary plaintext, and probes an endpoint to fingerprint the oracle that leaks padding validity.
tools.when: A web app returns distinguishable error codes on bad PKCS#7 padding and the app is yours to test — recover and forge CBC messages without the key.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/GDSSecurity/PadBuster && cd PadBuster && perl padBuster.pl https://app.example/decrypt -encoding 0

tools.name: cryptocrack
tools.desc: Crypto attacks + credential cracking — hash identify/crack with rules, RSA/AES/DH attacks, cipher auto-decode, XTS-CPA.
tools.when: Cracking/solving crypto-lab challenges and authorized recovery.

tools.name: hash_extender
tools.desc: Ron Bowes' C tool for the hash length-extension attack on MD4/MD5/RIPEMD-160/SHA-0/SHA-1/SHA-256/SHA-512/Whirlpool: given a secret-prefix hash, forges a valid hash for appended data without knowing the secret, iterating guessed secret lengths.
tools.when: A service signs 'secret || message' with a Merkle-Damgård hash (CTF or your own app) and you can control appended data - produce the new payload+signature pair the server accepts.

tools.name: Hashcat
tools.desc: GPU/CPU password cracker with 300+ attack modes and thousands of hash types; the full profile and masking/rule tooling live in the passwords domain. Linked here so crypto-work can confirm hash formats and modes.
tools.when: A recovered hash or extracted TGS ticket needs cracking; pair the hashcat mode from hashID with a rule/mask attack after confirming the target algorithm.
tools.install: sudo apt install hashcat && hashcat -m 1000 ntlm.hash rockyou.txt

tools.name: John the Ripper
tools.desc: CPU-first cracker (jumbo build) covering hundreds of hash formats including magic formats like Kerberoast/AS-REP tickets and encrypted OpenSSL/archive containers; full profile lives in the passwords domain.
tools.when: Cracking on CPU with the jumbo format set, or when a target format (gpg, ssh, rakefile) is only handled by John rather than Hashcat.
tools.install: sudo apt install john && john --wordlist=rockyou.txt hashes.txt

tools.name: RsaCtfTool
tools.desc: Python RSA multi-attack harness (60+ attacks): weak-key factorization (Fermat, Pollard rho, ECM, SIQS), lattice attacks on small d (Wiener, Boneh-Durfee), Hastad broadcast, shared-factor pools, ROCA, past-CTF/gimmick primes and Factordb integration; recovers the private key and/or decrypts files.
tools.when: Given a weak RSA public key and ciphertext (CTF, lab, keys you own) without knowing the weakness - run the default attack set, then target the specific winning attack.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/RsaCtfTool/RsaCtfTool && cd RsaCtfTool && pip3 install -r requirements.txt

tools.name: SageMath
tools.desc: Open-source mathematics system with built-in number theory used for RSA cryptanalysis: lattice basis reduction (LLL), Pollard p-1/p-ρ, discrete log, small-roots (Coppersmith), and private-key reconstruction from recovered parameters.
tools.when: When no one-shot tool covers the attack — hand-build a lattice basis, solve a modular equation, or derive d from partial parameters with a few lines of Sage.

tools.name: FactorDB
tools.desc: Online database of integer factorizations with a plain API (https://factordb.com/api?query=N) that returns a number's status (FF/C/PRP) and known factors, including factorized prime records.
tools.when: A modulus (or any big integer) may already be factored in the public corpus - script the API from curl; RsaCtfTool queries it automatically via --attack factordb.

tools.name: yafu
tools.desc: Automated integer-factoring command-line utility chaining trial division, Pollard, ECM, SIQS, and GNFS on numbers up to ~200 digits, with prebuilt Windows binaries and clean `factor(n)` syntax.
tools.when: A 256–1024-bit modulus you own that defeats online lookup — run `yafu 'factor(n)'` and let it auto-select the fastest factoring stage.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/bbuhrow/yafu && cd yafu && make yafu

tools.name: msieve
tools.desc: Quadratic-sieve and number-field-sieve library/demo for factoring integers up to ~120 digits (QS) and larger via GNFS, the classic engine behind CTF modulus-factorization writeups.
tools.when: Factoring tasks where yafu stalls or where you want the standalone QS/NFS engine; typically invoked from a script that feeds candidates one at a time.
tools.install: git clone https://github.com/radii/msieve && cd msieve && make

tools.name: rsatool
tools.desc: Small Python tool that reconstructs the full RSA key set (n, e, d, p, q, CRT params) and writes an OpenSSL-compatible PEM/DER private key from just (p, q) or (n, d), including n+dp-based factoring.
tools.when: After any attack yields p and q (or n+d): turn recovered parameters into a real private key file you can decrypt with, instead of rolling the CRT math by hand.
tools.install: wget -O rsatool.py https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ius/rsatool/master/rsatool.py && pip3 install gmpy2 pyasn1

tools.name: testssl.sh
tools.desc: Bash TLS cipher/protocol testing on any port: enumerates protocols and cipher suites, flags weaknesses (BEAST, heartbleed, ROBOT, TLS1.0/1.1, weak DHE), checks client simulation, and emits JSON/CSV/HTML.
tools.when: Full TLS configuration audit of an endpoint you own; the default single-line invocation yields findings graded vulnerable/weak/OK you can drop straight into a report.

tools.name: sslscan
tools.desc: Fast TLS cipher scanner built on a rewritten backend that detects SSLv2/SSLv3 and TLSv1.3 regardless of linked OpenSSL, flags CBC (POODLE), 3DES, RC4, NULL/weak ciphers, and weak DHE keys, with XML output.
tools.when: A quick closed-port cipher enumeration or legacy-protocol check where you want one line per cipher and color-coded strength annotations.
tools.install: sudo apt install sslscan && sslscan example.com:443

tools.name: SSLyze
tools.desc: Python TLS scanning library/CLI: cert, cipher suite, and elliptic-curve analysis plus known-attack checks (Heartbleed, ROBOT, CCS injection), with Mozilla-config comparison and JSON output for automation.
tools.when: Automated TLS gate in CI/CD or bulk scanning of many hosts; exit code flips on Mozilla 'intermediate' non-compliance, so it doubles as a regression check.
tools.install: pip3 install sslyze && python3 -m sslyze example.com

tools.name: OpenSSL
tools.desc: The de-facto CLI crypto Swiss-army knife: AES/ChaCha20/RSA/ECDSA encryption and decryption, key generation and parsing (PEM/DER), X.509 cert/genrsa/inspect, digests, and CMS/PKCS#7 envelopes in one command.
tools.when: Quick symmetric or asymmetric encrypt/decrypt of your files, dumping or inspecting keys and certificates, and validating algorithm behavior against a standards reference implementation.

tools.name: GnuPG
tools.desc: GNU Privacy Guard: full OpenPGP implementation for asymmetric and symmetric encryption, signing/verification, keyring management, and export/import interop with PGP e-mail workflows.
tools.when: Working with .gpg/PGP messages or OpenPGP keys where the PGP container format - not raw OpenSSL cipher - is expected.

tools.name: age
tools.desc: Simple, modern, audited file encryption (X25519, optional passphrase; hybrid post-quantum ML-KEM-768 since v1.3) with small explicit keys, no configuration and UNIX-style composability; interoperable Rust port is 'rage'.
tools.when: Modern default for encrypting archives/files you own end-to-end (backups, secrets transfer) when you want minimal friction and small keys over legacy OpenPGP keyrings.

tools.name: GnuTLS certtool
tools.desc: CLI from the GnuTLS project for X.509 certificate/key generation, PKCS#12 bundles, certificate and private-key inspection, and PKCS#11 token operations through a single binary.
tools.when: Generating or inspecting certificates and PKCS#12 files with readable options, or poking at PKCS#11 tokens, when OpenSSL's flag surface gets in the way.

tools.name: shadowvault
tools.desc: AES-256-GCM cryptographic secrets lifecycle manager for offensive ops — vaulted keys/creds, OPSEC zeroize on demand, team RBAC, migration tooling.
tools.when: When you need to hold many tool creds/keys safely during an engagement and wipe them fast at the end.
